title: Advanced Heap Variants
summary: Beyond the textbook binary heap: d-ary heaps, indexed/updatable priority queues for true decrease-key, and why Fibonacci heaps rarely get implemented.

slides.markdown:
This group's earlier topics established the binary heap as the default: array-backed, two children per node, O(log n) insert/extract, no true decrease-key. Each of those design choices is a specific point on a spectrum, and this closing topic covers the variants built for the bottlenecks a plain binary heap doesn't optimize for — more children per node, true in-place priority updates, and the theoretically-superior structures that almost nobody actually implements.

The throughline across all three: knowing a fancier structure exists and knowing whether it's actually worth reaching for are different skills, and the second one is what separates a candidate who's memorized trivia from one who reasons about the trade-off.

slides.subTitle: Fewer levels make sift-up cheaper, but each sift-down compares against more children
slides.markdown:
A **d-ary heap** generalizes the binary heap's "2 children per node" to **d children per node**. More children per node means the tree is shorter — height roughly log_d(n) instead of log_2(n) — so **sift-up** (which only ever compares against one parent per level) does fewer comparisons overall.

The trade-off: **sift-down** now has to compare against **d children** at each level to find the smallest (or largest), not just 2 — so each individual sift-down step costs more, even though there are fewer levels to sift through. The net effect depends on your insert-to-extract ratio: if inserts vastly outnumber extracts, a larger d can win; if extracts dominate, d=2 (the plain binary heap) or a small d is usually still better, since sift-down's per-level cost grows with d while sift-up's doesn't.

slides.subTitle: Raise d when inserts/decrease-key dominate; keep d=2 when extract-min dominates
slides.markdown:
| | Binary heap (d=2) | d-ary heap (d > 2) |
|---|---|---|
| Height | log₂ n | log_d n (shorter) |
| Sift-up cost | O(log₂ n) | O(log_d n) (cheaper) |
| Sift-down cost | O(log₂ n) with 2-way comparisons | O(d · log_d n) — more comparisons per level |
| Best for | balanced insert/extract workloads | insert-heavy or decrease-key-heavy workloads |

A concrete case where d > 2 wins: Prim's and Dijkstra's algorithms, implemented with an indexed heap supporting decrease-key, do far more decrease-key/insert-style operations than extract-min operations on dense graphs — some competitive-programming implementations specifically use d=4 for exactly this reason, since it measurably reduces total operations on that particular workload shape.

slides.subTitle: Tracking each element's heap position for true decrease-key
slides.markdown:
The `priority-queues-in-practice` topic covered lazy deletion as the practical workaround for the missing decrease-key operation. An **indexed heap** solves the actual problem instead of working around it: alongside the normal heap array, maintain a second array (or hash map) mapping each element's identity to its **current position** in the heap array.

With that position map kept correctly updated on every swap (sift-up and sift-down both need to update the map whenever they move an element), you can look up any element's current array index in O(1) and directly sift it up or down from there — true decrease-key in O(log n), no stale entries, no wasted heap space, unlike lazy deletion which can leave the heap holding more entries than live elements.

slides.subTitle: As Dijkstra and Prim actually need it
slides.markdown:
```python
class IndexedMinHeap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.heap = []          # array of (priority, elem)
        self.pos = {}            # elem -> current index in self.heap

    def _swap(self, i, j):
        self.heap[i], self.heap[j] = self.heap[j], self.heap[i]
        self.pos[self.heap[i][1]] = i
        self.pos[self.heap[j][1]] = j  # position map updated on every swap

    def decrease_key(self, elem, new_priority):
        i = self.pos[elem]
        self.heap[i] = (new_priority, elem)
        while i > 0 and self.heap[i] < self.heap[(i - 1) // 2]:
            self._swap(i, (i - 1) // 2)
            i = (i - 1) // 2
```

The critical detail versus a plain heap's sift-up: every swap must also update `self.pos`, or the index map drifts out of sync with the actual array and `decrease_key` starts looking up the wrong slot — silently corrupting future operations.

slides.subTitle: The conceptual idea behind O(1) amortized decrease-key
slides.markdown:
**Binomial heaps** structure themselves as a collection of binomial trees (each satisfying a specific size/shape rule) rather than one single tree, which gives O(log n) merge between two heaps — something a plain binary heap can't do efficiently at all.

**Fibonacci heaps** push further: by allowing a looser, "lazy" structure (deferring cleanup work until extract-min actually needs it, similar in spirit to lazy propagation in segment trees), they achieve O(1) **amortized** insert and decrease-key, with extract-min staying O(log n) amortized. This is the theoretical basis for the famous O(E + V log V) bound on Dijkstra's algorithm using a Fibonacci heap — strictly better than the O((E + V) log V) a plain binary heap gives.

slides.subTitle: Without being able to explain why it's rarely implemented in practice
slides.markdown:
A common interview overreach: citing "Dijkstra is O(E + V log V) with a Fibonacci heap" as if that's the practical recommendation, without being able to explain why almost nobody actually uses one. Fibonacci heaps have a large constant factor and complex bookkeeping (the lazy consolidation step during extract-min is intricate to implement correctly), and their amortized guarantees only pay off at scales where V and E are large enough that the asymptotic improvement outweighs the constant-factor overhead — a threshold many real workloads never reach.

The honest, complete answer names both facts: the Fibonacci heap gives the better **asymptotic** bound, and a plain binary heap (or an indexed d-ary heap) is what production code and competitive programmers actually reach for, because the constant-factor cost of Fibonacci heaps rarely pays off in practice. Citing only the impressive asymptotic number, without that caveat, reads as reciting a fact rather than understanding the trade-off.

slides.sectionTitle: When an indexed/Fibonacci heap earns its complexity
slides.subTitle: Vs when a plain heap + lazy deletion is good enough
slides.markdown:
| | Plain heap + lazy deletion | Indexed heap | Fibonacci heap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Implementation effort | trivial | moderate (position map) | high (lazy consolidation) |
| Decrease-key | not supported (workaround only) | true, O(log n) | true, O(1) amortized |
| Extra space | can exceed O(n) with stale entries | O(n) | O(n) |
| When it's the right call | most interview and production code | dense graphs, many decrease-key calls, correctness-sensitive space budgets | rarely — mostly of theoretical/academic interest, or extreme-scale specialized systems |

The practical decision rule closing this group: default to a plain heap with lazy deletion unless you have a specific, measured reason not to (stale-entry space genuinely matters, or correctness requires no phantom entries) — reach for an indexed heap in that case. Reach for a Fibonacci heap essentially never in applied work; know it exists and know its asymptotic claim, but recognize that citing it as your practical answer is usually the wrong move in an interview.
